claim: Plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDCs) constitute a rare type of immune cell with multifaceted functions.
source: Plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDCs) constitute a rare type of immune cell with multifaceted functions, but their potential use as a cell-based immunotherapy is challenged by the scarce cell numbers that can be extracted from blood.
evidence: This is a general characterization statement in the abstract that is supported by established scientific knowledge about pDCs.

claim: The potential use of pDCs as a cell-based immunotherapy is challenged by the scarce cell numbers that can be extracted from blood.
source: Plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDCs) constitute a rare type of immune cell with multifaceted functions, but their potential use as a cell-based immunotherapy is challenged by the scarce cell numbers that can be extracted from blood.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge in the field and is a known limitation of pDC-based therapies.

claim: Using optimized conditions combined with implementation of HSPC pre-expansion, an average of 465 million HSPC-derived pDCs can be generated starting from 100,000 cord blood-derived HSPCs.
source: Using optimized conditions combined with implementation of HSPC pre-expansion, we generate an average of 465 million HSPC-derived pDCs (HSPC-pDCs) starting from 100,000 cord blood-derived HSPCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing cell yields from the optimized protocol.

claim: The protocol allows HSPC-pDC generation from whole-blood HSPCs.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrate that such protocol allows HSPC-pDC generation from whole-blood HSPCs, and these cells display a pDC phenotype and function.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing successful generation of pDCs from whole blood HSPCs.

claim: HSPC-pDCs generated from whole blood display a pDC phenotype and function.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrate that such protocol allows HSPC-pDC generation from whole-blood HSPCs, and these cells display a pDC phenotype and function.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing phenotypic and functional characterization of whole blood-derived HSPC-pDCs.

claim: Using GMP-compliant medium results in a remarkable loss of TLR7/9 responses.
source: Using GMP-compliant medium, we observe a remarkable loss of TLR7/9 responses, which is rescued by ascorbic acid supplementation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing TLR responses in different media conditions.

claim: Ascorbic acid supplementation rescues the loss of TLR7/9 responses observed with GMP-compliant medium.
source: Using GMP-compliant medium, we observe a remarkable loss of TLR7/9 responses, which is rescued by ascorbic acid supplementation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing restoration of TLR responses upon ascorbic acid addition.

claim: Ascorbic acid induces transcriptional signatures associated with pDC-specific innate immune pathways.
source: Ascorbic acid induces transcriptional signatures associated with pDC-specific innate immune pathways, suggesting an undescribed role of ascorbic acid for pDC functionality.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data showing differential gene expression upon ascorbic acid supplementation.

claim: Ascorbic acid has an undescribed role for pDC functionality.
source: Ascorbic acid induces transcriptional signatures associated with pDC-specific innate immune pathways, suggesting an undescribed role of ascorbic acid for pDC functionality.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observed transcriptional changes and functional improvements.

claim: This constitutes the first protocol for generating pDCs from whole blood.
source: This constitutes the first protocol for generating pDCs from whole blood and lays the foundation for investigating HSPC-pDCs for cell-based immunotherapy.
evidence: This is a claim of novelty based on the authors' knowledge of the field.

claim: pDCs are capable of producing high levels of type I interferon (IFN) upon exposure to virus-derived nucleic acids that are recognized by Toll-like receptor (TLR) 7 and TLR9.
source: In addition to conventional dendritic cell (cDC) functions, pDCs are capable of producing high levels of type I interferon (IFN) upon exposure to virus-derived nucleic acids that are recognized by Toll-like receptor (TLR) 7 and TLR9 (Swiecki and Colonna, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: pDCs effectively produce pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines such as IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8, TNFα, and ligands for CXCR3 (CXCL9, CXCL10, and CXCL11).
source: Though the signature cytokine secreted by activated pDCs are type I IFNs, pDCs also effectively produce other pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines such as IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8, TNFα, and ligands for CXCR3 (CXCL9, CXCL10, and CXCL11) (Tel, 2012; van Beek, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Several preclinical studies have confirmed the immunotherapeutic potential of pDCs for the treatment of cancer through a multifaceted stimulation of the immune system.
source: Several preclinical studies have confirmed the immunotherapeutic potential of pDCs for the treatment of cancer through a multifaceted stimulation of the immune system (Aspord, 2014; Drobits, 2012; Wu, 2017; Belounis, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to preclinical studies.

claim: Two clinical trials have shown that autologous tumor antigen-loaded pDCs induce antitumoral responses and significantly improved clinical outcome for melanoma and prostate cancer patients.
source: Importantly, two clinical trials have shown that autologous tumor antigen-loaded pDCs induce antitumoral responses and significantly improved clinical outcome for melanoma and prostate cancer patients, respectively (Tel, 2013; Westdorp, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical trial publications.

claim: A comparison of pDCs and cDCs suggests that pDCs are superior to cDCs at attracting CD8+ T cells, γ/δ T cells, and CD56+ NK cells to sites of melanoma.
source: In one of these trials, a mixture of pDCs and cDCs was used, and a follow-up comparison of these two cell types suggests that pDCs are superior to cDCs at attracting CD8+ T cells, γ/δ T cells, and CD56+ NK cells to sites of melanoma (van Beek, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a follow-up study.

claim: pDCs constitute 0.1% ± 0.07% of PBMCs in peripheral blood.
source: While attempts have been made to translate the use of pDCs into a clinical immunotherapeutic setting, their use has been severely impeded by their rarity within peripheral blood (0.1% ± 0.07% of PBMCs) (Ueda, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation providing quantitative data on pDC frequency.

claim: pDCs have short ex vivo survival.
source: Coupled with their short ex vivo survival, they are very difficult to study and modulate as a population (Zhan, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to literature on pDC survival.

claim: HSPC-derived pDCs can be generated from different sources of HSPCs, including cord blood and mobilized peripheral blood.
source: These studies demonstrate that HSPC-derived pDCs (HSPC-pDCs) can be generated from different sources of HSPCs, including cord blood (CB) and mobilized peripheral blood.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies demonstrating pDC generation from different HSPC sources.

claim: Adoptive transfer therapy of autologous HSPC-pDCs is challenging due to low cell yield and the requirement for patients to undergo granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF)-induced HSPC mobilization.
source: Although some improvements in different methods of pDC generation have been achieved, adoptive transfer therapy of autologous HSPC-pDCs is still challenging due to low cell yield and the requirement for patients to undergo granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF)-induced HSPC mobilization.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of current limitations in the field.

claim: A combination of growth factors, cytokines, and small molecules (Flt3-L, TPO, SCF, IL-3, and SR1) supported HSPC expansion and differentiation into immature HSPC-pDCs.
source: We identified that a combination of growth factors, cytokines, and small molecules (Flt3-L, TPO, SCF, IL-3, and SR1) supported HSPC expansion and differentiation into immature HSPC-pDCs.
evidence: This is supported by data from the authors' previous publication.

claim: Following a 21-day culture period, an average of 35% of the culture was HSPC-pDCs.
source: Following a 21-day culture period, an average of 35% of the culture was HSPC-pDCs, which could be enriched to near purity using immunomagnetic depletion of non-pDCs.
evidence: This is supported by data from the authors' previous publication.

claim: HSPC-pDCs could be enriched to near purity using immunomagnetic depletion of non-pDCs.
source: Following a 21-day culture period, an average of 35% of the culture was HSPC-pDCs, which could be enriched to near purity using immunomagnetic depletion of non-pDCs.
evidence: This is supported by data from the authors' previous publication.

claim: To generate a mature and functional phenotype, the HSPC-pDCs culture required priming by exposure to type I and II IFNs.
source: Most importantly, we showed that to generate a mature and functional phenotype, the HSPC-pDCs culture required priming by exposure to type I and II IFNs (Laustsen, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by data from the authors' previous publication.

claim: Culturing HSPCs ex vivo at low-density culture conditions stimulates the transition of HSPCs into the cell cycle, thereby supporting the expansion of HSPCs.
source: Prior work has demonstrated that culturing HSPCs ex vivo at LD culture conditions stimulates the transition of HSPCs into the cell cycle, thereby supporting the expansion of HSPCs (Charlesworth, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The low-density protocol led to a higher expansion of HSPCs compared to the standard protocol during the 21-day culture.
source: During the 21-day culture, we observed that the LD protocol led to a higher expansion of HSPCs compared to the standard protocol (Figure 1a and Figure 1—figure supplement 1a–c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Starting from 2 × 10^5 HSPCs, an average number of 1.5 × 10^9 (± 0.7 × 10^9) total cells were obtained with the low-density protocol compared to 0.055 × 10^9 (± 0.001 × 10^9) in the standard condition.
source: Starting from 2 × 105 HSPCs, we obtained an average number of 1.5 × 109 (± 0.7 × 109) total cells compared to 0.055 × 109 (± 0.001 × 109) in the standard condition.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the low-density culture experiments.

claim: The low-density culture protocol highly increased HSPC-pDC numbers.
source: Next, we isolated HSPC-pDCs using immunomagnetic depletion of non-pDCs. Importantly, we found that the LD culture protocol also highly increased HSPC-pDC numbers.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing yields between protocols.

claim: Starting from 2 × 10^5 HSPCs, the average yield of isolated HSPC-pDCs was 201 × 10^6 (± 58.7 × 10^6) with low-density protocol versus 10.4 × 10^6 (± 2.3 × 10^6) HSPC-pDCs in the standard condition.
source: Starting from 2 × 105 HSPCs, the average yield of isolated HSPC-pDCs was 201 × 106 (± 58.7 × 106) versus 10.4 × 106 (± 2.3 × 106) HSPC-pDCs in the standard condition (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: The low-density protocol yields an average of 1005 (± 293) HSPC-pDCs per single CD34+ HSPC, which is an average improvement of 19-fold over the standard condition.
source: This is an average yield of 1005 (± 293) HSPC-pDCs per single CD34+ HSPC, which is an average improvement of 19-fold over the standard condition.
evidence: This is calculated from experimental data comparing the two protocols.

claim: The culture density did not affect the viability of the cells during the 21-day culture period.
source: The culture density did not affect the viability of the cells during the 21-day culture period (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c), nor did it influence the fraction of HSPC-pDCs among the total cells that were generated at day 21 (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c.

claim: The culture density did not influence the fraction of HSPC-pDCs among the total cells that were generated at day 21.
source: The culture density did not affect the viability of the cells during the 21-day culture period (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c), nor did it influence the fraction of HSPC-pDCs among the total cells that were generated at day 21 (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: A small decrease in viability of the isolated HSPC-pDCs from the low-density culture was detected.
source: However, a small decrease in viability of the isolated HSPC-pDCs from the LD culture was detected (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1d.

claim: Isolated HSPC-pDCs require priming by adding type I and II IFNs to the culture medium to become functionally active and responsive to TLR7 and TLR9 agonists.
source: Previously, we have shown that isolated HSPC-pDCs require a priming by adding type I and II IFNs to the culture medium to become functionally active and responsive to TLR7 and TLR9 agonists.
evidence: This is supported by data from the authors' previous publication.

claim: HSPC-pDCs generated under low-density conditions showed no difference in type I IFN response when stimulated with a TLR7 agonist compared to standard conditions.
source: Evaluation of type I IFN responses of HSPC-pDCs generated under LD conditions versus standard conditions showed no difference when stimulated with a TLR7 agonist and a minor improvement for the LD condition when stimulated with a TLR9 agonist (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: HSPC-pDCs generated under low-density conditions showed a minor improvement in type I IFN response when stimulated with a TLR9 agonist compared to standard conditions.
source: Evaluation of type I IFN responses of HSPC-pDCs generated under LD conditions versus standard conditions showed no difference when stimulated with a TLR7 agonist and a minor improvement for the LD condition when stimulated with a TLR9 agonist (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Phenotypic analysis of pDC surface markers showed no obvious difference between the standard and low-density culture conditions.
source: Phenotypic analysis of pDC surface markers by flow cytometry of the isolated HSPC-pDCs (Lin-CD11c-CD123+CD303+) showed no obvious difference between the two culture conditions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1e–h).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1e–h.

claim: SFEM II significantly promoted the proliferation of HSPCs compared to RPMI with serum.
source: We found that SFEM II significantly promoted the proliferation of HSPCs compared to RPMI with serum (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Starting from 1 × 10^5 HSPCs, an average of 2.4 × 10^9 (± 0.6 × 10^9) total cells were generated at day 21 with SFEM II versus 0.7 × 10^9 (± 0.4 × 10^9) total cells for RPMI.
source: Starting from 1 × 105 HSPCs, an average of 2.4 × 109 (± 0.6 × 109) total cells were generated at day 21 with SFEM II versus 0.7 × 109 (± 0.4 × 109) total cells for RPMI (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The high expansion rate using SFEM II translated to a significantly higher yield of isolated HSPC-pDCs at all three time points of isolation.
source: The high expansion rate using SFEM II also translated to a significantly higher yield of isolated HSPC-pDCs at all three time points of isolation, with a maximum of 580 × 106 HSPC-pDCs (± 123 × 106) HSPC-pDCs isolated after 21 days of culture using SFEM II (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: A maximum of 580 × 10^6 HSPC-pDCs (± 123 × 10^6) were isolated after 21 days of culture using SFEM II.
source: The high expansion rate using SFEM II also translated to a significantly higher yield of isolated HSPC-pDCs at all three time points of isolation, with a maximum of 580 × 106 HSPC-pDCs (± 123 × 106) HSPC-pDCs isolated after 21 days of culture using SFEM II (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: After 16 days of differentiation, 100 × 10^6 (± 22.2 × 10^6) HSPC-pDCs could be isolated starting from only 0.1 × 10^6 HSPC.
source: Even after 16 days of differentiation, 100 × 106 (± 22.2 × 106) HSPC-pDCs could be isolated starting from only 0.1 × 106 HSPC.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the SFEM II culture experiments.

claim: The transition to SFEM II did not affect the proportion of HSPC-pDCs in the cell culture.
source: The transition to SFEM II did not affect the proportion of HSPC-pDCs in the cell culture as similar percentages of HSPC-pDCs were observed across all three isolation time points, indicating that pDCs differentiate continuously during the culture (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: pDCs differentiate continuously during the culture.
source: The transition to SFEM II did not affect the proportion of HSPC-pDCs in the cell culture as similar percentages of HSPC-pDCs were observed across all three isolation time points, indicating that pDCs differentiate continuously during the culture (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of similar percentages of HSPC-pDCs across time points.

claim: No difference in viability of the isolated HSPC-pDCs was observed at any time point or condition.
source: Importantly, no difference in viability of the isolated HSPC-pDCs was observed at any time point or condition (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Cells generated using SFEM II displayed a higher capacity to produce type I IFN upon TLR7 and TLR9 activation.
source: We next performed TLR7 and TLR9 activation assays of the produced HSPC-pDCs, which showed that cells generated using SFEM II displayed a higher capacity to produce type I IFN (Figure 2d and e).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2d and 2e.

claim: HSPC-pDCs that had been isolated at earlier time points produced significantly more type I IFN upon TLR9 activation.
source: Interestingly, we observed that HSPC-pDCs that had been isolated at earlier time points produced significantly more type I IFN upon TLR9 activation, suggesting that there is a balance between proliferation potential and the immunotherapeutic properties of HSPC-pDCs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing TLR9 responses at different isolation time points.

claim: There is a balance between proliferation potential and the immunotherapeutic properties of HSPC-pDCs.
source: Interestingly, we observed that HSPC-pDCs that had been isolated at earlier time points produced significantly more type I IFN upon TLR9 activation, suggesting that there is a balance between proliferation potential and the immunotherapeutic properties of HSPC-pDCs.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed data on timing of isolation and functionality.

claim: Phenotypic analysis of the pDC-related surface markers CD123 and CD303 showed no differences across time points and conditions.
source: Phenotypic analysis of the pDC-related surface markers CD123 and CD303 on lin-CD11c- cells showed no differences across time points and conditions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1d–g).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1d–g.

claim: Ex vivo culturing of HSPCs at low densities combined with the small molecules UM171 and SR1 promotes self-renewal of primitive hematopoietic progenitor cells and long-term repopulating hematopoietic stem cells.
source: Recent publications have found that ex vivo culturing of HSPCs at low densities combined with the small molecules UM171 and SR1 promotes self-renewal of primitive hematopoietic progenitor cells and long-term repopulating hematopoietic stem cells (LT-HSCs) (Charlesworth, 2018; Fares, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent publications.

claim: HSPCs expanded significantly during pre-expansion with an average of 78 (± 14)-fold expansion for the 8-day pre-expansion.
source: HSPCs were cultured at LD concentrations (0.1–0.5 × 106 cells/mL) for up to 8 days (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a), during which the cells expanded significantly with an average of 78 (± 14)-fold expansion for the 8-day pre-expansion (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b, c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1b, c.

claim: Upon thawing, expanded HSPCs remained viable and positive (>95%) for the HSPC surface marker CD34+.
source: Upon thawing, expanded HSPCs remained viable and positive (>95%) for the HSPC surface marker CD34+ with no difference compared to HSPCs that had not been expanded (Figure 3—figure supplement 1d–h).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1d–h.

claim: Surface expression levels (MFI) of CD34 appeared to increase during the first four initial days of expansion, and then decrease again over time.
source: However, surface expression levels (MFI) of CD34 appeared to increase during the first four initial days of expansion, and then decrease again over time (Figure 3—figure supplement 1h).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1h.

claim: HSPCs that had undergone pre-expansion for 6 and 8 days showed decreased expansion during pDC differentiation.
source: We observed that HSPCs that had undergone pre-expansion for 6 and 8 days showed decreased expansion during pDC differentiation, but viabilities throughout differentiation remained high for all conditions (Figure 3b and Figure 3—figure supplement 2i–k).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b and Figure 3—figure supplement 2i–k.

claim: Viabilities throughout differentiation remained high for all pre-expansion conditions.
source: We observed that HSPCs that had undergone pre-expansion for 6 and 8 days showed decreased expansion during pDC differentiation, but viabilities throughout differentiation remained high for all conditions (Figure 3b and Figure 3—figure supplement 2i–k).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b and Figure 3—figure supplement 2i–k.

claim: The stagnated growth correlated with increased numbers of adherent cells during later days of pDC differentiation.
source: The stagnated growth correlated with increased numbers of adherent cells during later days of pDC differentiation, and these adherent cells displayed a morphology with long protrusions indicative of cDCs or macrophages (data not shown).
evidence: This is based on observational data, though the data is not shown.

claim: Adherent cells displayed a morphology with long protrusions indicative of cDCs or macrophages.
source: The stagnated growth correlated with increased numbers of adherent cells during later days of pDC differentiation, and these adherent cells displayed a morphology with long protrusions indicative of cDCs or macrophages (data not shown).
evidence: This is an inference based on morphological observations.

claim: Prolonged pre-expansion affects differentiation and the proliferative capacity of hematopoietic progenitors, which in turn may influence pDC differentiation.
source: This indicates that prolonged pre-expansion affects differentiation and the proliferative capacity of hematopoietic progenitors, which in turn may influence pDC differentiation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed effects of prolonged pre-expansion.

claim: Lower yields of immunomagnetically separated HSPC-pDCs were observed upon prolonged pre-expansion, particularly when combined with 21 days of pDC differentiation.
source: Accordingly, when initiating HSPC-pDC differentiation from the same starting cell numbers, lower yields of immunomagnetically separated HSPC-pDCs were observed upon prolonged pre-expansion, particularly when combined with 21 days of pDC differentiation (data not shown).
evidence: This is based on experimental data, though the data is not shown.

claim: A progressive decline in the percentage of HSPC-pDCs of the total cell population was observed as the cells had been pre-expanded for longer durations.
source: A progressive decline in the percentage of HSPC-pDCs of the total cell population was also observed as the cells had been pre-expanded for longer durations (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: With a 4-day pre-expansion of HSPCs and a 21-day pDCs differentiation, 3.1 × 10^9 (± 1.2 × 10^9) HSPC-pDCs could be generated versus 0.9 × 10^9 (± 0.3 × 10^9) HSPC-pDCs when no pre-expansion was applied.
source: With a 4-day pre-expansion of HSPCs and a 21-day pDCs differentiation, 3.1 × 109 (± 1.2 × 109) HSPC-pDCs could be generated versus 0.9 × 109 (± 0.3 × 109) HSPC-pDCs when no pre-expansion was applied.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from pre-expansion experiments.

claim: Early pDC isolation at day 16 yielded an average of 4.7 × 10^8 (± 1.1 × 10^8) HSPC-pDCs when a 4-day pre-expansion was applied.
source: Similarly, early pDC isolation at day 16 yielded an average of 4.7 × 108 (± 1.1 × 108) HSPC-pDCs when a 4-day pre-expansion was applied (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: The functional capacity of HSPC-pDCs to secrete type I IFN upon activation with TLR7 or TLR9 agonists was highly affected when cells were pre-expanded for a prolonged time.
source: Interestingly, we found that the functional capacity of HSPC-pDCs to secrete type I IFN upon activation with TLR7 or TLR9 agonists was highly affected when cells were pre-expanded for a prolonged time (Figure 3e and f).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3e and 3f.

claim: The TLR9-mediated type I IFN response was significantly decreased when applying 6 or 8 days of pre-expansion.
source: This was in particular evident for the TLR9-mediated type I IFN response, which was significantly decreased when applying 6 or 8 days of pre-expansion.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing TLR9 responses across pre-expansion durations.

claim: Surface expression of CD123 and CD303 was not affected by culture duration.
source: Conversely, surface expression of CD123 and CD303 was not affected by culture duration (Figure 3—figure supplement 2l–n).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2l–n.

claim: There is a trend of reduced functionality with longer time in culture, which might reflect a type of functional exhaustion during prolonged cell culture.
source: Overall, these data show a trend of reduced functionality with longer time in culture, which might reflect a type of functional exhaustion during prolonged cell culture.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed trend in functionality.

claim: When a limited period of pre-expansion of 4 days is combined with an early isolation of HSPC-pDCs of 16 days, high yields of functional HSPC-pDCs can be generated.
source: Collectively, we here show that prolonged pre-expansion, as well as extended pDC differentiation culture, drastically affects the functionality of generated HSPC-pDCs. Nevertheless, when a limited period of pre-expansion of 4 days is combined with an early isolation of HSPC-pDCs of 16 days, high yields of functional HSPC-pDCs can be generated.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on pre-expansion and isolation timing.

claim: Expansion of cells during pDC differentiation was highly reduced when HSPCs were cultured in cGMP medium.
source: Interestingly, we found that expansion of cells during pDC differentiation was highly reduced when HSPCs were cultured in cGMP medium (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Cell viabilities remained high throughout the culture period with cGMP medium.
source: However, cell viabilities remained high throughout the culture period, but the number of HSPC-pDCs that could be isolated from the culture was reduced in accordance with the lower expansion (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b and c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1b and c.

claim: The number of HSPC-pDCs that could be isolated from the culture was reduced in accordance with the lower expansion when using cGMP medium.
source: However, cell viabilities remained high throughout the culture period, but the number of HSPC-pDCs that could be isolated from the culture was reduced in accordance with the lower expansion (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b and c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1b and c.

claim: Viabilities of isolated HSPC-pDCs and their proportion of the total cell population were largely unaffected by cGMP medium.
source: Viabilities of isolated HSPC-pDCs and their proportion of the total cell population were largely unaffected (Figure 4—figure supplement 1d and e), leading us to believe that their functionality would remain unaffected.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1d and e.

claim: Cells cultured in the two cGMP-compliant media were found to either completely lack or have drastically reduced capacity to produce type I IFN upon TLR7 or TLR9 agonist activation.
source: Remarkably, while isolated HSPC-pDCs from all three culture conditions phenotypically expressed the pDC markers CD123 and CD303 to the same extent, cells cultured in the two cGMP-compliant media were found to either completely lack or have drastically reduced capacity to produce type I IFN upon TLR7 or TLR9 agonist activation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1f and g).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1f and g.

claim: Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) is an essential vitamin in humans known to have pleiotropic functions in cellular biology, including immune cell function and hematopoiesis.
source: Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) is an essential vitamin in humans known to have pleiotropic functions in cellular biology, including immune cell function and hematopoiesis (Manning, 2013; Huijskens, 2014; Huijskens, 2015; Bowie and O'Neill, 2000; Agathocleous, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Ascorbic acid has been shown to be involved in type I IFN immune responses.
source: Interestingly, AA has been shown to be involved in type I IFN immune responses.
evidence: This is supported by knowledge from the literature.

claim: Transgenic mice lacking the capacity to synthesize ascorbic acid show diminished capacity to produce type I IFN upon TLR activation and influenza infection.
source: Unlike humans, mice can synthesize AA but transgenic mice lacking the capacity to synthesize AA actually show diminished capacity to produce type I IFN upon TLR activation and influenza infection. This indicates that AA may play a role in either TLR activity or pDC development (Kim, 2013; Geber et al., 1975).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on transgenic mice.

claim: Ascorbic acid may play a role in either TLR activity or pDC development.
source: Unlike humans, mice can synthesize AA but transgenic mice lacking the capacity to synthesize AA actually show diminished capacity to produce type I IFN upon TLR activation and influenza infection. This indicates that AA may play a role in either TLR activity or pDC development (Kim, 2013; Geber et al., 1975).
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on observations in transgenic mice.

claim: Medium supplement with ascorbic acid can increase DC yield during ex vivo differentiation from HSPC.
source: While no reports provide clear evidence of a role in pDC development of function, one study does find that medium supplement with AA can increase DC yield during ex vivo differentiation from HSPC, but its significance in pDC functionality was not investigated (Thordardottir, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: DC medium supplemented with ascorbic acid significantly promoted expansion during HSPC-pDC differentiation up to similar level as the SFEM II culture condition.
source: We found that DC medium supplemented with AA significantly promoted expansion during HSPC-pDC differentiation up to similar level as the SFEM II culture condition (expansion of 33,554-fold [± 11,664] for DC medium+ AA versus 13,456-fold [± 6953] for DC medium alone) (Figure 4a and Figure 4—figure supplement 2h–i).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4a and Figure 4—figure supplement 2h–i.

claim: Addition of ascorbic acid significantly improved viability of expanding HSPCs during culture, particularly during later stages of culture (day 12+).
source: Moreover, addition of AA significantly improved viability of expanding HSPCs during culture, particularly during later stages of culture (day 12+) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2j).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2j.

claim: The viability of HSPC-pDCs isolated at day 21 was significantly increased upon ascorbic acid addition compared to DC medium alone (92.0% ± 3.4% versus 72.8% ± 3.2%).
source: Additionally, we also found the viability of HSPC-pDCs isolated at day 21 to be significantly increased upon AA addition compared to DC medium alone (92.0% ± 3.4% versus 72.8% ± 3.2%) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2k).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2k.

claim: The yield of HSPC-pDCs was significantly increased upon ascorbic acid supplementation for HSPC-pDCs isolated at day 21 (1.0 × 10^9 ± 0.4 × 10^9 HSPC-pDCs for DC medium + AA versus 0.5 × 10^9 ± 0.3 × 10^9 for DC medium alone per 0.1 × 10^6 CD34+ HSPCs).
source: Accordingly, the yield of HSPC-pDCs was significantly increased upon AA supplementation for HSPC-pDCs isolated at day 21 (1.0 × 109 ± 0.4 × 109 HSPC-pDCs for DC medium + AA versus 0.5 × 109 ± 0.3 × 109 for DC medium alone per 0.1 × 106 CD34+ HSPCs), without affecting the percentage of HSPC-pDCs of the total population of cells (Figure 4b and c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4b and 4c.

claim: Ascorbic acid supplementation did not affect the percentage of HSPC-pDCs of the total population of cells.
source: Accordingly, the yield of HSPC-pDCs was significantly increased upon AA supplementation for HSPC-pDCs isolated at day 21 (1.0 × 109 ± 0.4 × 109 HSPC-pDCs for DC medium + AA versus 0.5 × 109 ± 0.3 × 109 for DC medium alone per 0.1 × 106 CD34+ HSPCs), without affecting the percentage of HSPC-pDCs of the total population of cells (Figure 4b and c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4b and 4c.

claim: HSPC-pDCs generated from the ascorbic acid culture consistently elicited a robust type I IFN response in contrast to DC medium alone for cells isolated both on days 16 and 21.
source: Interestingly, we found that HSPC-pDCs generated from the AA culture consistently elicited a robust type I IFN response in contrast to DC medium alone for cells isolated both on days 16 and 21 (Figure 4d and e).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4d and 4e.

claim: The type I IFN response of HSPC-pDCs generated with ascorbic acid exceeded the response of HSPC-pDCs generated using SFEM II medium.
source: The response was even found to exceed the response of HSPC-pDCs generated using SFEM II medium.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing responses across media conditions.

claim: HSPC-pDCs isolated at 16 days of culture displayed improved capacity to produce type I IFN upon TLR7 or TLR9 activation compared to cells isolated at day 21.
source: As previously observed, HSPC-pDCs isolated at 16 days of culture displayed improved capacity to produce type I IFN upon TLR7 or TLR9 activation compared to cells isolated at day 21 (Figure 4d and e).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4d and 4e.

claim: The capacity of HSPC-pDCs to secrete the pro-inflammatory proteins TNF-α and IL-6 upon TLR7 and TLR9 activation was rescued when ascorbic acid was present.
source: Moreover, we found that the capacity of HSPC-pDCs to secrete the pro-inflammatory proteins TNF-α and IL-6 upon TLR7 and TLR9 activation was also rescued when AA was present (Figure 4—figure supplement 2l and m).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2l and m.

claim: pDCs isolated from ascorbic acid-supplemented culture at day 16 displayed lower expression levels of CD303.
source: Upon analysis of surface expression of the markers CD123 and CD303, we found that pDCs isolated from AA-supplemented culture at day 16 displayed lower expression levels of CD303.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data on surface marker expression.

claim: No statistical significance was observed in the percentage of cells expressing CD303 between the conditions.
source: However, no statistical significance was observed in the percentage of cells expressing CD303 between the conditions (Figure 4—figure supplement 2n–p).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2n–p.

claim: A small distinct population of HSPC-pDCs showing high surface expression of CD123 was observed upon ascorbic acid supplementation.
source: A small distinct population of HSPC-pDCs showing high surface expression of CD123 was observed upon AA supplementation (Figure 4—figure supplement 2q).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2q.

claim: The pDC marker HLA-DR is highly expressed in HSPC-pDCs upon IFN priming, correlating with the capacity of the cells to activate T cells through antigen presentation.
source: Previously, we have shown that the pDC marker HLA-DR is highly expressed in HSPC-pDCs upon IFN priming, correlating with the capacity of the cells to activate T cells through antigen presentation (Laustsen, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by data from the authors' previous publication.

claim: HLA-DR was upregulated upon IFN priming in HSPC-pDCs generated from DC medium.
source: We similarly found HLA-DR to be upregulated upon IFN priming in HSPC-pDCs generated from DC medium.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data on HLA-DR expression.

claim: No statistically significant difference in HLA-DR expression was observed upon ascorbic acid addition.
source: However, no statistically significant difference was observed upon AA addition (Figure 4—figure supplement 2r and s).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2r and s.

claim: A distinct subset of precursor conventional dendritic cells (pre-DC) exists in peripheral blood.
source: Numerous studies have described that a distinct subset of precursor conventional dendritic cells (pre-DC) exists in peripheral blood (See, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to literature describing pre-DCs.

claim: Pre-DCs have functional and phenotypical similarities with blood pDCs, including surface expression of CD123, CD303, and CD304, and the capacity to produce type I IFN upon TLR7 or TLR9 agonist stimulation.
source: Due to functional and phenotypical similarities with blood pDCs, including surface expression of CD123, CD303, and CD304, and the capacity to produce type I IFN upon TLR7 or TLR9 agonist stimulation, this subpopulation has inadvertently been considered as pDCs (Ito, 2006; See, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature describing pre-DC characteristics.

claim: Pre-DCs express CD2, CD5, and CD33, and secrete IL-12 upon TLR activation.
source: Notably, pre-DCs have been shown to express CD2, CD5, and CD33, and secrete IL-12 upon TLR activation (See, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to literature describing pre-DC markers and function.

claim: HSPC-pDCs differentiated with or without ascorbic acid were unable to produce IL-12 upon TLR7 and TLR9 agonist exposure.
source: However, HSPC-pDCs differentiated with or without AA were unable to produce IL-12 upon TLR7 and TLR9 agonist exposure and had no detectable levels of CD2 on the surface (Figure 4—figure supplement 2t and u).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2t and u.

claim: HSPC-pDCs differentiated with or without ascorbic acid had no detectable levels of CD2 on the surface.
source: However, HSPC-pDCs differentiated with or without AA were unable to produce IL-12 upon TLR7 and TLR9 agonist exposure and had no detectable levels of CD2 on the surface (Figure 4—figure supplement 2t and u).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2t and u.

claim: cDCs or pre-DCs are not present in the immunomagnetically selected HSPC-pDC population.
source: This supports that cDCs or pre-DCs are not present in the immunomagnetically selected HSPC-pDC population (Laustsen, 2018).
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of pre-DC markers and supported by previous work.

claim: Ascorbic acid is essential for ex vivo differentiation of pDCs from HSPCs when using cGMP-compliant medium by increasing expansion of HSPCs and improving viability of expanding cells and isolated HSPC-pDCs, as well as functionality of isolated HSPC-pDCs.
source: Altogether, our results demonstrate that AA is essential for ex vivo differentiation of pDCs from HSPCs when using cGMP-compliant medium by both increasing expansion of HSPCs and improving viability of expanding cells and isolated HSPC-pDCs, as well as functionality of isolated HSPC-pDCs.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion supported by multiple experimental observations.

claim: 1250 genes were differentially expressed upon ascorbic acid addition; 916 genes upregulated and 334 genes downregulated.
source: Overall, we found that 1250 genes were differentially expressed upon AA addition; 916 genes upregulated and 334 genes downregulated (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: A gene ontology analysis of the differentially expressed genes showed a significant enrichment of biological processes related to the immune system, including gene ontologies for innate immune sensing and responses to viruses.
source: A gene ontology analysis of the differentially expressed genes showed a significant enrichment of biological processes related to the immune system, including gene ontologies for innate immune sensing and responses to viruses (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 5b.

claim: Several genes associated with pDC development and function were significantly upregulated by ascorbic acid, including TCF4 (E2-2), SPIB, IRF7, IRF8, TLR7, TLR8, TLR9, UNC93B1, PACSIN-1, GMZB, CLEC4C, and LILRA4.
source: Separately, we also found several genes associated with pDC development and function to be significantly upregulated by AA. In particular, we found the 'master regulator' of pDC development and function TCF4 (E2-2), and TCF-regulated genes, including SPIB, IRF7, IRF8, TLR7, TLR8, TLR9, UNC93B1, PACSIN-1, GMZB, CLEC4C, and LILRA4 to be significantly upregulated (Figure 5c; Cisse, 2008; Cheng, 2015; Ghosh, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5c and citations to literature on these genes.

claim: Several genes associated with innate immune functions of TLR7 and TLR9 were activated upon ascorbic acid addition, including IRF5, IRF7, IRF8, TLR7, TLR9, MyD88, TRAF3, UNC93B1, LAMP5, PACSIN-1, RSAD2, SLC15A4, and SPP1.
source: Moreover, we found several genes associated with innate immune functions of TLR7 and TLR9 to be activated upon AA addition. These included IRF5, IRF7, IRF8, TLR7, TLR9, MyD88, TRAF3, UNC93B1, LAMP5, PACSIN-1, RSAD2, SLC15A4, and SPP1 (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: Several genes are known to control assembly and trafficking of TLR7 and TLR9 to late endosomes, including UNC93B1, PLSCR1, SLC15A4, and LAMP5.
source: Of these genes, several are known to control assembly and trafficking of TLR7 and TLR9 to late endosomes, including Unc-93 homolog B1 (UNC93B1), phosholipase scrambase 1 (PLSCR1), solute carrier family 15 member A4 (SLC15A4), and BAD-LAMP (LAMP5) (Combes, 2017; Blasius, 2010; Talukder, 2012; Pelka, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on TLR trafficking.

claim: MyD88, PACSIN1, IRF5, IRF7, RSAD2, and SPP1 are directly involved in TLR7 and TLR9 downstream signaling.
source: Of the remaining genes, myeloid differentiation primary response protein MyD88 (MyD88), protein kinase C and casein kinase substrate in neurons 1 (PACSIN1), interferon regulatory factor 5 (IRF5), IRF7, viperin (RSAD2), and osteopontin (SPP1) are directly involved in TLR7 and TLR9 downstream signaling, possibly explaining the observed lack of TLR7 or TLR9 activation upon absence of AA (Figure 5c; Saitoh, 2011; Kawai, 2004; Honda, 2005; Shinohara, 2006; Schoenemeyer, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data and citations to literature on TLR signaling.

claim: General surface markers specifically associated with pDCs were upregulated by ascorbic acid, including CD303 (CLEC4C), CD304 (NRP1), CD123 (IL3RA), and CD85g (LILRA4).
source: General surface markers specifically associated with pDCs were similarly found to be upregulated by AA, including CD303 (CLEC4C), CD304 (NRP1), CD123 (IL3RA), and CD85g (LILRA4) (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: Multiple genes associated with antigen processing and presentation were elevated transcriptionally upon ascorbic acid addition, particularly CD40, CD86, and genes within the HLA family of receptors.
source: We also found multiple genes associated with antigen processing and presentation to be elevated transcriptional upon AA addition, particularly CD40, CD86, and genes within the HLA family of receptors (Figure 5c and Figure 5—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5c and Figure 5—figure supplement 1a.

claim: No enrichment for gene ontologies relating to ROS and oxidative stress was identified among differentially expressed genes upon ascorbic acid addition.
source: Since AA is a strong antioxidant and scavenges reactive oxygen species (ROS), we finally analyzed gene ontologies relating to ROS and oxidative stress. However, we did not identify an enrichment for any related differentially expressed genes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Ascorbic acid upregulates multiple genes associated with pDC development and immunological functions.
source: Collectively, these data show that AA upregulates multiple genes associated with pDC development and immunological functions.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: Two clinical trials using adoptive transfer of autologous pDCs have shown clinical benefit.
source: This has also limited the use of pDCs for immunotherapy, but importantly, two independent clinical trials using adoptive transfer of autologous pDCs have shown clinical benefit (Tel, 2013; Westdorp, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical trial publications.

claim: In a phase I clinical trial, Tel et al. vaccinated stage IV melanoma patients with autologous pDCs loaded with tumor peptides, which improved overall survival, with 45% of patients still being alive after 2 years, compared to 10% in the matched control patients treated with conventional chemotherapy.
source: In one phase I clinical trial, Tel et al. vaccinated stage IV melanoma patients with autologous pDCs loaded with tumor peptides derived from the melanoma-associated antigens, gp100 and tyrosinase. The therapy improved overall survival, with 45% of patients still being alive after 2 years, compared to 10% in the matched control patients treated with conventional chemotherapy (Tel, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a clinical trial publication.

claim: Westdorp et al. found in a phase IIa clinical trial that vaccination using cDCs and pDCs in combination, loaded with tumor-associated antigens, improved the clinical outcome of patients with castration-resistant prostate cancer.
source: Similarly, Westdorp et al. found in a phase IIa clinical trial that vaccination using cDCs and pDCs in combination, loaded with the tumor-associated antigens NY-ESO-1, MAGE-C2, and MUC1, improved the clinical outcome of patients with castration-resistant prostate cancer (Westdorp, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a clinical trial publication.

claim: In both clinical trials, antigen-loaded pDCs were found to effectively induce B and CD8+ T cell anti-tumor-specific responses in patients, while being well-tolerated and safe (grade 1–2 toxicities).
source: In both clinical trials, antigen-loaded pDCs were found to effectively induce B and CD8+ T cell anti-tumor-specific responses in patients, while being well-tolerated and safe (grade 1–2 toxicities) (Tel, 2013; Westdorp, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical trial publications.

claim: The principal drawback of pDC-based therapy was the maximum feasible dose of only 0.3–3 × 10^6 pDCs per vaccination, and only three vaccinations at biweekly intervals were performed.
source: The principal drawback, which was also highlighted in these studies, was the maximum feasible dose of only 0.3–3 × 106 pDCs per vaccination, and only three vaccinations at biweekly intervals were performed (Tel, 2013; Westdorp, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical trial publications.

claim: In clinical trials utilizing monocyte-derived cDCs, patients received 4–8 vaccine regiments with biweekly intervals with predefined moDC doses ranging from 10 to 30 × 10^6 cells.
source: In contrast, in clinical trials utilizing monocyte-derived cDCs (moDCs), patients received 4–8 vaccine regiments with biweekly intervals with predefined moDC doses ranging from 10 to 30 × 106 cells (Boudewijns, 2020; Okada, 2011; Ribas, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical trial publications.

claim: The FDA-approved autologous dendritic cell immunotherapy, Provenge (sipuleucel-T), comprises three vaccination doses of a minimum of 50 million dendritic cells each, and some patients have been treated with doses as high as 1.3 billion dendritic cells.
source: Similarly, the FDA-approved autologous dendritic cell immunotherapy, Provenge (sipuleucel-T), comprises three vaccination doses of a minimum of 50 million dendritic cells each, and some patients have been treated with doses as high as 1.3 billion dendritic cells (Small, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to literature on Provenge.

claim: There is an unmet need for a clinical manufacturing protocol that allows high and robust numbers of pDCs to be generated.
source: Consequently, there is an unmet need for a clinical manufacturing protocol that allows high and robust numbers of pDCs to be generated.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of current limitations in the field.

claim: The platform allows the generation of consistent high numbers of autologous HSPC-pDCs that can be used for multiple vaccine regiments and that can be extracted from easily accessible whole blood.
source: We believe that our platform meets this need by allowing the generation of consistent high numbers of autologous HSPC-pDCs that can be used for multiple vaccine regiments and that can be extracted from easily accessible whole blood.
evidence: This is a claim about the capabilities of the developed platform based on the experimental results.

claim: pDCs can be generated using CB CD34+ HSPCs or mobilized peripheral blood CD34+ HSPCs.
source: We and other groups have previously demonstrated that pDCs can be generated using CB CD34+ HSPCs or mobilized peripheral blood CD34+ HSPCs (mPB-HSPCs; Diaz-Rodriguez, 2017; Thordardottir, 2017; Demoulin, 2012; Olivier, 2006; Curti, 2001; Thordardottir, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The major drawback of CB HSPCs is the need for an HLA match between donor and recipient.
source: While CB HSPCs possess a great stem cell potential, the major drawback is the need for an HLA match between donor and recipient.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about CB HSPC transplantation.

claim: Obtaining mPB-HSPCs requires multiple injections of G-CSF usually over four consecutive days, followed by apheresis and large-scale CD34 immunomagnetic selection.
source: Obtaining mPB-HSPCs requires multiple injections of G-CSF usually over four consecutive days, followed by apheresis and large-scale CD34 immunomagnetic selection.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about HSPC mobilization procedures.

claim: The procedure for obtaining mPB-HSPCs is time-consuming, costly, requires access to expensive equipment, and is associated with inconvenience to the donor and side effects such as bone pain.
source: Thus, the procedure is time-consuming, costly, requires access to expensive equipment, and is associated with inconvenience to the donor and side effects such as bone pain.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about HSPC mobilization procedures.

claim: Natural pDCs from peripheral blood have a half-life of only about 24 hr when cultured ex vivo.
source: Natural pDCs from peripheral blood have been used, but very few numbers can be isolated from a buffy coat, and the cells have a half-life of only about 24 hr when cultured ex vivo (Grouard, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to literature on pDC survival.

claim: Generated HSPC-pDCs show superior survival versus peripheral blood-derived pDCs.
source: We have previously shown that generated HSPC-pDCs show superior survival versus peripheral blood-derived pDCs, indicating that HSPC-pDCs are more suitable to receive modifications, for example, antigen loading and activation, which are required for immunotherapy in a clinical setting.
evidence: This is supported by data from the authors' previous work.

claim: HSPC-pDCs are more suitable to receive modifications, for example, antigen loading and activation, which are required for immunotherapy in a clinical setting.
source: We have previously shown that generated HSPC-pDCs show superior survival versus peripheral blood-derived pDCs, indicating that HSPC-pDCs are more suitable to receive modifications, for example, antigen loading and activation, which are required for immunotherapy in a clinical setting.
evidence: This is an inference based on the superior survival of HSPC-pDCs.

claim: Thordardottir et al. previously reported a yield of 1.6 million HSPC-pDCs starting from 100,000 mPB-HSPCs.
source: Thordardottir et al. previously reported a yield of 1.6 million HSPC-pDCs starting from 100,000 mPB-HSPCs (Thordardottir, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Using the same starting cell number and same duration of pDC differentiation, with no pre-expansion included, an average of 306 million HSPC-pDCs were generated amounting to a 191-fold improvement over Thordardottir et al.'s method.
source: Using the same starting cell number and same duration of pDC differentiation, with no pre-expansion included, we generated an average of 306 million HSPC-pDCs amounting to a 191-fold improvement, albeit their starting material was mPB-HSPCs and ours CB-HSPCs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing yields to previous studies.

claim: Isolating pDCs earlier improved their capacity to produce type I IFN upon stimulation with synthetic TLR7 or TLR9 agonists.
source: Importantly, we found that isolating pDCs earlier improved their capacity to produce type I IFN upon stimulation with synthetic TLR7 or TLR9 agonists.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing functionality at different isolation time points.

claim: Prolonged pDC differentiation leads to a dysfunctional type I IFN response, possibly due to pDC exhaustion.
source: This indicates that prolonged pDC differentiation leads to a dysfunctional type I IFN response, possibly due to pDC exhaustion, albeit more research needs to be conducted to further characterize this phenotype.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed functional decline with prolonged culture.

claim: Using the shortened 16-day differentiation protocol and no HSPC pre-expansion, up to 152 million HSPC-pDCs were generated from 100,000 CB-HSPCs.
source: Using our shortened 16-day differentiation protocol and no HSPC pre-expansion, we generated up to 152 million HSPC-pDCs from 100,000 CB-HSPCs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the optimized protocol.

claim: Using the pre-expansion strategy, an average of 8 million HSPC-pDCs were generated starting from 100,000 cHSPCs.
source: Using our pre-expansion strategy, we were able to generate an average of 8 million HSPC-pDCs starting from 100,000 cHSPCs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from whole blood HSPC experiments.

claim: With an average number of 1.1 × 10^6 cHSPCs in a standard buffy coat from 450 mL of blood, an average of 88 million HSPC-pDCs could be generated.
source: With an average number of 1.1 × 106 cHSPCs in a standard buffy coat from 450 mL of blood, this would allow for an average of 88 million HSPC-pDCs to be generated in a manner that is minimally invasive to the patient.
evidence: This is calculated from experimental data on cHSPC isolation and pDC generation.

claim: The cHSPC-pDCs can be cryopreserved, allowing repeated vaccine regiments.
source: The cHSPC-pDCs can in turn be cryopreserved, allowing repeated vaccine regiments (Figure 7).
evidence: This is based on the capability to cryopreserve cells as demonstrated in the methods.

claim: The numbers of generated HSPC-pDCs highly exceed the number of natural pDCs that can be obtained from peripheral blood even when using leukapheresis.
source: These numbers of generated cells highly exceed the number of natural pDCs that can be obtained from peripheral blood even when using leukapheresis (Tel, 2013; Westdorp, 2019).
evidence: This is based on comparison with clinical trial data on pDC isolation.

claim: An additional advantage of HSPC-pDCs over natural pDCs is that HSPC-pDCs are amenable to genetic modifications.
source: An additional advantage of HSPC-pDCs over natural pDCs is that HSPC-pDCs are amenable to genetic modifications (Laustsen, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by data from the authors' previous publication.

claim: CRISPR/Cas gene editing could potentially allow amplification of the response of pDCs or render them resistant to inhibitory tumor signals.
source: This potentially allows CRISPR/Cas gene editing to amplify the response of pDCs or render them resistant to inhibitory tumor signals.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential applications of gene editing.

claim: Further preclinical studies are warranted on the potency of the generated HSPC-pDCs to induce anti-tumoral responses before the protocol can be translated and implemented into clinical practice.
source: However, further preclinical studies are warranted on the potency of the generated HSPC-pDCs to induce anti-tumoral responses before the protocol can be translated and implemented into clinical practice.
evidence: This is a statement about the need for future research.

claim: An average of 1.1 × 10^6 CD34+ cHSPCs (± 0.6 × 10^6 cHSPCs) were obtained from buffy coats, corresponding to 2457 cHSPCs (± 1307 cHSPCs) per mL of blood.
source: We obtained an average number of 1.1 × 106 CD34+ cHSPCs ( ± 0.6 × 106 cHSPCs), corresponding to 2457 cHSPCs (± 1307 cHSPCs) per mL of blood in line with previous observations (Beyer and Muench, 2017; Eidenschink, 2012; Figure 6—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1a and citations to previous studies.

claim: During pre-expansion, cHSPCs expanded 4.6-fold (± 1.5-fold) and retained CD34 expression.
source: During pre-expansion, cHSPCs expanded 4.6-fold (± 1.5-fold) and retained CD34 expression (Figure 6—figure supplement 1b–j).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1b–j.

claim: During the 16 days of pDC differentiation, a 257-fold (± 91-fold) expansion of total cells was observed for non-pre-expanded cHSPC versus 192-fold (± 126-fold) for cHSPC pre-expanded for 4 days.
source: During the 16 days of pDC differentiation, we observed a 257-fold (± 91-fold) expansion of total cells for non-pre-expanded cHSPC versus 192-fold (± 126-fold) for cHSPC pre-expanded for 4 days (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6a.

claim: When starting from 1 × 10^5 cHSPCs, the total yield of cHSPC-pDCs following immunomagnetic selection was 3.5 × 10^6 cHSPC-pDCs (± 2.9 × 10^6) without pre-expansion.
source: When starting from 1 × 105 cHSPCs, the total yield of cHSPC-pDCs following immunomagnetic selection was 3.5 × 106 cHSPC-pDCs (± 2.9 × 106) without pre-expansion.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from whole blood HSPC experiments.

claim: Using an optimized setup with 4 days of pre-expansion, an average yield of 8.0 × 10^6 cHSPC-pDCs (± 4.5 × 10^6) was observed.
source: Using an optimized setup with 4 days of pre-expansion, an average yield of 8.0 × 106 cHSPC-pDCs (± 4.5 × 106) was observed (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6b.

claim: For the pre-expanded condition, 80 cHSPC-pDCs were generated per single cHSPC.
source: For the pre-expanded condition, this corresponds to 80 cHSPC-pDCs generated per single cHSPC.
evidence: This is calculated from experimental data.

claim: Of the total cell population generated, cHSPC-pDCs accounted for an average of 23% for pre-expanded cHSPC.
source: Of the total cell population generated, cHSPC-pDCs accounted for an average of 23% for pre-expanded cHSPC (Figure 6c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6c.

claim: The observed pre-expansion, differentiation potential, and yield were less for cHSPCs compared to CB-HSPCs, whereas the frequency of pDCs obtained was similar.
source: As expected, the observed pre-expansion, differentiation potential, and yield were less for cHSPCs compared to CB-HSPCs, whereas the frequency of pDCs obtained was similar.
evidence: This is based on comparison of experimental data between cHSPCs and CB-HSPCs.

claim: cHSPC-pDCs were capable of producing type I IFN upon TLR7 or TLR9 stimulation.
source: Importantly, cHSPC-pDCs were capable of producing type I IFN upon TLR7 or TLR9 stimulation, and the cells displayed a pDC surface phenotype similar to HSPC-pDCs derived from CB (Figure 6d and e and Figure 6—figure supplement 1k–n).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6d, 6e, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1k–n.

claim: cHSPC-pDCs displayed a pDC surface phenotype similar to HSPC-pDCs derived from CB.
source: Importantly, cHSPC-pDCs were capable of producing type I IFN upon TLR7 or TLR9 stimulation, and the cells displayed a pDC surface phenotype similar to HSPC-pDCs derived from CB (Figure 6d and e and Figure 6—figure supplement 1k–n).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6d, 6e, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1k–n.

claim: Ascorbic acid was required for cHSPC-pDC TLR7 and TLR9-mediated type I IFN production.
source: As we had previously observed, AA was required for cHSPC-pDC TLR7 and TLR9-mediated type I IFN production (Figure 6—figure supplement 1o).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1o.

claim: High numbers of functional HSPC-pDCs can be generated from a simple blood sample.
source: Collectively, we demonstrate that high numbers of functional HSPC-pDCs can be generated from a simple blood sample, which highly simplifies the procedure for generating pDCs for basic studies of pDC biology and for immunotherapeutic purposes.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion supported by experimental data from whole blood experiments.

claim: The developed procedure highly simplifies the procedure for generating pDCs for basic studies of pDC biology and for immunotherapeutic purposes.
source: Collectively, we demonstrate that high numbers of functional HSPC-pDCs can be generated from a simple blood sample, which highly simplifies the procedure for generating pDCs for basic studies of pDC biology and for immunotherapeutic purposes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the demonstrated capability to generate pDCs from whole blood.
